lesson.title: The Power Chain Rule: n Times u to the n Minus 1, Times u Prime
lesson.summary: When a whole expression is raised to a power, the derivative multiplies the ordinary power rule by the derivative of what is inside the parentheses.
lesson.body:
The power rule for a simple variable, d/dx[x^n] = n x^(n-1), only works when the base is literally x. The moment the base becomes a more complicated expression, such as (5x - 2)^3 or (x^2 + 4)^(-1), that formula alone gives a wrong answer, because it ignores the fact that the base itself is changing with x at its own rate. The power chain rule repairs this by pairing the power rule with the chain rule formula f'(g(x)) g'(x), and it is one of the most frequently used rules in an entire calculus course because so many functions are built from something raised to a power.

The rule: d/dx[u^n] = n u^(n-1) times du/dx, where u is any differentiable function of x. This is exactly the composition derivative rule with the outside function chosen as f(t) = t^n, so f'(t) = n t^(n-1); nothing new is being invented here, the power rule derivative is simply being combined with the chain rule formula covered earlier. Recognizing composition is the first step in every one of these problems, since u must be correctly identified as whatever expression sits inside the parentheses before n u^(n-1) can even be written down.

Differentiate y = (5x - 2)^3. Here u = 5x - 2 and n = 3, so du/dx = 5. The power chain rule gives dy/dx = 3(5x-2)^2 times 5 = 15(5x-2)^2. Verify by full expansion as a second method: (5x-2)^3 = 125x^3 - 150x^2 + 60x - 8. Differentiating term by term gives 375x^2 - 300x + 60. Now expand the chain rule answer: 15(5x-2)^2 = 15(25x^2 - 20x + 4) = 375x^2 - 300x + 60. The two methods match exactly, confirming the rule. A second, quicker example: for y = (x^2+1)^4, u = x^2+1 and du/dx = 2x, so dy/dx = 4(x^2+1)^3 times 2x = 8x(x^2+1)^3.

The same pattern handles negative and fractional exponents once du/dx is computed correctly, though those extensions are the focus of the general power rule ahead; for now, the key habit is recognizing u as whatever is inside the parentheses being raised to a power and never forgetting the trailing du/dx factor. Forgetting that factor is the single most common power chain rule mistake, and it is exactly why the worked example above included a full expansion check: without the factor of 5, the answer 3(5x-2)^2 alone would not match the expanded derivative, and the discrepancy would only show up once both sides were compared term by term.

This rule will reappear constantly, including inside the combining chain rule topic that pairs it with product and quotient rules, because so many calculus expressions involve something raised to a power nested inside a larger computation. Getting comfortable naming u, computing n u^(n-1), and multiplying by du/dx as one fluid motion is one of the highest leverage skills in a first calculus course, and it pays off again immediately in the trig, exponential, and log chain rules that follow, all of which share this exact same three step rhythm.
